newsitem.title: USA: Mexico's Zedillo sees improving U.S.-Mexico ties.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Zedillo sees improving U.S.-Mexico ties.

text.p: Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo said on Thursday his country's ties with the United States should grow stronger, but a free trade agreement spanning the Western Hemisphere awaited a U.S. commitment.

In a speech to business and local political leaders here, Zedillo noted expanding trade and other relationships between the two neighbours, helped by the North American Free Trade Agreement enacted four years ago.
"It is an immense relationship economically and geographically," he said. "And culturally and socially, it is an intense relationship."
"But we believe free trade should be a reality not only for a small group of countries in the Americas," Zedillo said in response to a question about the future of Hemispheric trade.

"Mexico has been ready from the very beginning to start negotiations (on a Hemisphere-wide trade pact), but domestic political matters in the United States have impeded the beginning of these negotiations.

"We hope that, not so far in the future, the U.S. administration will be provided with fast-track authority, so we can start talking seriously about this," he said, referring to the practice of U.S. negotiators gaining Congress' consent not to tinker with any new signed agreements.
In the meantime, Mexico has not stood idle and has extended its policy of open trade beyond NAFTA, Zedillo said.
"Mexico is doing its best, and quite successfully, to open free trade with other countries in the Americas," he said, citing free trade pacts with Chile, Venezuela, Colombia, Bolivia and Costa Rica.

"Quite likely we will quite soon be in a position to sign free trade agreements with other countries in Central America," he said, adding that Mexico announced on Wednesday it had set conditions with the European Union for negotiations on establishing a free trade agreement.
In his speech, Zedillo urged his audience to visit and invest in Mexico, which he said was making progress politically as well as economically.

"Mexico has achieved democratic normality ... (that) will temper extremism and foster dialogue," Zedillo said, speaking proudly of July 6 elections in which two opposition parties made broad gains against his ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI).

As for Mexico's domestic economy, Zedillo predicted that this year's growth would be similar to last year's expansion of slightly more than 5 percent. He projected employment growth of 1 million new jobs a year, lower interest rates, and single-digit inflation at the very least by the year 2000.
